claims.text: Unmodified Ti6Al4V (TC4) has an alpha-plus-beta dual-phase microstructure.
Unmodified TC4 has low hardness and poor friction and wear properties.
A nanostructured, ceramic-reinforced laser-clad surface coating will improve the hardness of TC4.
A nanostructured, ceramic-reinforced laser-clad surface coating will improve the wear resistance of TC4.
The coating will retain the beneficial properties of TC4.
Tuning laser power, scanning speed, and feedstock composition can promote strong metallurgical bonding between the coating and TC4.
Tuning laser power, scanning speed, and feedstock composition can produce controlled microstructural refinement.
The intervention will form a composite coating containing dispersed hard ceramic phases and a refined microstructure.
The coating microstructure will transition smoothly into the TC4 substrate.
Ceramic reinforcements in the coating impede dislocation motion.
Ceramic reinforcements reduce surface deformation.
Impeded dislocation motion and reduced surface deformation increase surface hardness and wear resistance.
Because laser cladding modifies the surface, it will not alter the bulk properties of TC4.
Laser-clad TC4 will have significantly higher surface hardness than untreated TC4.
Laser-clad TC4 will have a lower wear rate than untreated TC4.
Laser-clad TC4 will maintain toughness comparable to untreated TC4.
Laser-clad TC4 will maintain corrosion resistance comparable to untreated TC4.
The predicted improvements apply under high-contact-stress conditions at temperatures up to 600 degrees Celsius.
The exact hardness and wear improvements and the long-term stability under cyclic loading remain undetermined.
Failure to achieve both a 20% hardness increase and a 20% wear-rate decrease relative to untreated TC4, or coating adhesion failure or deleterious defects, would falsify the hypothesis.
